lessons.title: Language Core
lessons.explanation:
# 01 · Language Core

C# is a big language with a small centre. This module is that centre: how a
value gets copied, what `null` really means now that the compiler has an
opinion about it, why money is `decimal` and never `double`, and how to say
a branching rule as an expression instead of a staircase of `if`s.

None of it is exotic. All of it shows up in the first hour of reading any
real .NET codebase, and every item here is a bug someone shipped this week.

## The mental model

### 1 · Values are copied, references are shared

Every type in .NET is one of two kinds, and the kind decides what happens
when you assign it or pass it to a method.

```csharp
struct Point { public int X; }      // a VALUE: the variable holds the data
class Box { public int X; }         // a REFERENCE: the variable holds an arrow

var a = new Point { X = 1 };
var b = a;  b.X = 99;               // a.X is still 1 — b got a copy

var c = new Box { X = 1 };
var d = c;  d.X = 99;               // c.X is now 99 — same object
```

`int`, `double`, `decimal`, `bool`, `char`, `DateTime`, `Guid` and every
`struct` are values. `string`, arrays, `List<T>`, and every `class` and
`record` are references. (`string` is a reference type that *behaves* like
a value, because it is immutable — you can never observe the sharing.)

### 2 · Nullable is a conversation with the compiler

In a modern project `string` means "never null" and `string?` means "might
be". The compiler tracks it and warns you; it does not enforce it at
runtime.

```csharp
string? maybe = GetName();
int length = maybe.Length;        // warning: may be null
int safe = maybe?.Length ?? 0;    // no warning, no crash
```

`?.` skips the member access and gives `null`; `??` supplies a fallback;
`??=` assigns only if the target is null. There is a fourth operator, `!`
("I know better"), and reaching for it is almost always how a
`NullReferenceException` gets born.

### 3 · A switch expression is a value, not a jump

```csharp
var band = grams switch
{
    < 0 => "invalid",
    0 => "free",
    < 1000 => "small",
    _ => "pallet",
};
```

Arms are tried top to bottom, first match wins, and the whole thing produces
a value — so the compiler can prove every path returns one. Patterns
compose: relational (`< 1000`), type (`is int n`), property
(`{ Weight: 0 }`), and the combinators `and`, `or`, `not`.

### 4 · There are three numeric worlds

| type | base | use it for | never use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int` / `long` | 2 | counts, ids, indexes | anything divided |
| `double` | 2 | measurements, physics, ratios | money |
| `decimal` | 10 | money, tax, anything a human audits | tight loops, science |

`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in `double` and *is* `0.3m` in `decimal`. That is not a
bug in .NET; it is base-2 fractions doing what base-2 fractions do.

## The details that bite

1. **`int / int` is integer division, whatever you assign it to.**
   `double avg = 7 / 2;` is `3.0`. The cast has to happen before the
   division: `(double)7 / 2`.
2. **`Math.Round` uses banker's rounding by default.**
   `Math.Round(0.5)` is `0`, not `1` — correct for statistics, wrong for
   an invoice. Say `MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero` when you mean money.
3. **`==` on `object` compares references.** Two boxed `1`s are two
   objects. Use `Equals(a, b)` — the static form, which is null-safe on
   both sides.
4. **`ToLower()` uses the current culture.** In Turkish, lowercasing `I`
   does not give `i`, so `a.ToLower() == b.ToLower()` compares different
   strings on a Turkish machine. For keys and ids, use
   `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` or `ToLowerInvariant`.
5. **A blank string is not null and is still missing.** `name != null`
   passes for `"   "`. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the check you meant.
6. **An `out` parameter must be assigned on every path**, including the
   failure path. A `Try` method that fails and leaves the old value in
   place hands the caller a stale number.
7. **Boxing allocates.** `object o = 42;` puts 42 on the heap. In a hot
   loop that is a garbage-collection problem, which is why the BCL has a
   generic overload of nearly everything.
8. **Mutable structs are a trap.** You mutate a copy and the change
   vanishes. Make structs `readonly` and return modified copies with
   `with`.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-count-vowels.cs` | ★☆☆ | a string walk, and your first meeting with culture |
| 02 | `02-value-vs-reference.cs` | ★☆☆ | what a copy copies — struct vs class, and a "copy" that isn't |
| 03 | `03-numbers-that-lie.cs` | ★☆☆ | integer division, decimal money, rounding a half cent |
| 04 | `04-nullable-without-fear.cs` | ★★☆ | null, blank, present — and the operators that tell them apart |
| 05 | `05-strings-that-compare.cs` | ★★☆ | ordinal vs culture, and normalising a key you will look up |
| 06 | `06-pattern-matching.cs` | ★★☆ | shipping rules as switch expressions, not if-staircases |
| 07 | `07-tuples-and-deconstruction.cs` | ★☆☆ | two answers from one call, named and deconstructed |
| 08 | `08-out-and-ref.cs` | ★★☆ | the Try pattern, done properly, plus ref and discards |
| 09 | `09-boxing-and-equality.cs` | ★★★ | a settings bag of `object`, and what equals means in it |
| 10 | `10-spans-without-allocating.cs` | ★★★ | parsing with `ReadOnlySpan<char>` — no Split, no Substring |

Do the warm-ups and core in order; 01 through 08 is the spine. The two
stretch files are the ones an interviewer uses to separate "writes C#" from
"knows what the runtime is doing" — worth the time, skippable on a first
pass.

```
dotnet run exercises/01-count-vowels.cs   # yours
dotnet run solutions/01-count-vowels.cs   # the answer + walkthrough
dotnet run ../verify.cs 01                # the whole module
dotnet run ../progress.cs 01              # the scoreboard
```

---

**Stuck?** `cheatsheets/csharp-language.md` (syntax, operators, patterns) · **Self-check:** `quizzes/01-language-core.md` · **Next:** `bootcamp/02-methods-and-delegates`

csbootcamp/01-language-core/01-count-vow.instructions:
**Concepts:** strings · loops · char  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A tag cleaner needs to know how "sayable" a slug is, and the crude
proxy is the vowel count. Write CountVowels: how many characters of
the text are a, e, i, o or u, in either case.

    CountVowels("hello")   → 2
    CountVowels("HELLO")   → 2
    CountVowels("rhythm")  → 0

A string is an IEnumerable<char>, so you can foreach over it.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/01-count-vow.explanation:
A string is a sequence of chars, so `foreach (var c in text)` is the
plain loop — and because LINQ works on any IEnumerable<T>, the whole
thing collapses to one Count with a predicate. Both are idiomatic;
the LINQ version is what you would write in review.
The case question has two answers and only one of them is right.
`char.ToLower(c)` uses the CURRENT CULTURE, which is a real bug in
Turkish locales (where lowercasing 'I' does not give 'i'). Comparing
against a set of both cases, or using `char.ToLowerInvariant`, is
culture-proof. This is your first meeting with a rule that runs
through the whole track: text operations that "obviously" do not
depend on locale usually do.
The classic wrong turn is `text.Count(c => "aeiou".Contains(c))`
without handling case — green on "hello", red on "HELLO".

csbootcamp/01-language-core/02-value-vs-.instructions:
**Concepts:** value types · reference types · struct vs class  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Two types are defined at the BOTTOM of this file: Point is a struct
(a value), Box is a class (a reference). Passing one to a method
copies the value; passing the other copies the arrow, not the thing.

Write three methods and let the tests show you the difference:

    MovedRight(p, 3)  → a NEW point 3 to the right; p is untouched
    Rename(box, "b")  → renames the CALLER'S box, returns nothing
    CopyOf(box)       → a NEW box with the same name, independent

hint: `p with { X = p.X + dx }` builds a modified copy of a record
struct. For CopyOf you want `new Box(...)`, not `box`.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/02-value-vs-.explanation:
One rule explains all six tests: a variable of a VALUE type holds the
data; a variable of a REFERENCE type holds an arrow to data that
lives elsewhere. Assigning or passing copies whatever the variable
holds — the data in the first case, the arrow in the second.
So MovedRight cannot mutate the caller's Point even if it tries: it
was handed a copy. `with` makes that explicit by producing a new
value rather than editing one. Rename CAN mutate the caller's Box,
because both names point at the same object.
CopyOf is the interesting one. Returning `box` would compile, pass
the "same name" test, and fail the next one — a "copy" that is the
original is the shared-reference bug, and it is the single most
common data bug in any language with references.
Equality follows the same split. A record struct gets value equality
for free, so two Points with the same numbers are Equal. A plain
class gets reference equality, so two Boxes with the same name are
two different objects — which is why `==` on your own classes is
almost never what a business rule means.
In .NET this shows up as: structs for small immutable values
(Point, DateOnly, Money), classes for things with identity (a
Customer, an Order). Mutable structs are a trap for exactly this
reason — you mutate a copy and the change disappears.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/03-numbers-t.instructions:
**Concepts:** integer division · double vs decimal · rounding  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Three small calculations, each with a trap C# will not warn you
about:

    Average(7, 2)            → 3.5    (not 3)
    WithTax(19.99m, 21m)     → 24.19m (money, rounded to cents)
    SafeDivide(10, 0)        → 0      (no exception)

WithTax takes a price and a tax rate in PERCENT, adds the tax, and
rounds to two decimal places. A total ending .005 rounds UP — that
is what an invoice does, and it is not what .NET does by default.

hint: `int / int` is integer division no matter what you assign it
to. Math.Round has an overload that takes a MidpointRounding.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/03-numbers-t.explanation:
Average: `total / count` where both are int is INTEGER division —
7 / 2 is 3, and the fraction is gone before the double ever sees it.
The assignment target does not change how the division is done. Cast
one operand first: `(double)total / count`.
WithTax: money is decimal, never double. `decimal` is base 10, so
0.1m + 0.2m is exactly 0.3m, while 0.1 + 0.2 as doubles is
0.30000000000000004. The other half is the rounding MODE: .NET's
default is banker's rounding (MidpointRounding.ToEven), so
Math.Round(0.075m, 2) gives 0.08 but Math.Round(0.045m, 2) gives
0.04 — correct for statistics, wrong for an invoice. Say what you
mean: MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero.
SafeDivide: integer division by zero throws DivideByZeroException —
unlike double division, which quietly gives Infinity. Guard the
denominator.
The classic wrong turn is writing `double Average(int a, int b) =>
a / b;` and testing it with 10 and 5, which passes. Every
integer-division bug in production was tested with numbers that
happened to divide evenly.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/04-nullable-.instructions:
**Concepts:** nullable reference types · ?? · ?. · blank strings  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Three helpers that all deal with "the value might not be there", the
single most common shape in line-of-business code:

    DisplayName("Ada", "Lovelace")  → "Ada Lovelace"
    DisplayName("Ada", null)        → "Ada"
    DisplayName(null, null)         → "(unknown)"
    DisplayName("  ", "")           → "(unknown)"

    TotalLength(["ab", null, "c"])  → 3
    FirstNonBlank([null, " ", "x"]) → "x"   (none found → "")

A value that is present but blank counts as missing everywhere here.
That is a product decision, and it is the one users expect.

hint: string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace answers "missing?" in one call.
`??` supplies a fallback; `?.` skips a member access on null.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/04-nullable-.explanation:
The lesson is that C# has THREE states where you were thinking of
two: null, blank, and present. `first != null` is not the check the
product wants — a name of "  " passes it and prints as nothing. Ask
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` and the three states collapse into the
two you actually branch on.
DisplayName then becomes: keep the parts that are present, join with
a space, and fall back when nothing survived. Building a list and
joining beats nested if/else because the rule ("skip the missing
ones") is stated once instead of once per combination.
TotalLength shows `?.` and `??` doing their real job: `v?.Length`
is null when v is null rather than throwing, and `?? 0` turns the
absence into the identity element for addition. That pairing — null
-conditional to skip, null-coalescing to default — is most of what
nullable code looks like.
Nullable reference types are compile-time only. `string?` and
`string` are the same type at runtime; the ? is a promise the
compiler checks and a caller in an older project can break. Guard
at the boundary anyway.
Classic wrong turns: `first + " " + last` (double spaces and
trailing spaces when a part is missing) and the null-forgiving `!`
operator used to silence a warning you have not actually handled.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/05-strings-t.instructions:
**Concepts:** StringComparison · ordinal vs culture · normalising keys  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A tag system. Tags are compared case-insensitively but are otherwise
exact — trailing spaces are a different tag, because a user typed
them and a dictionary key does not forgive:

    SameTag("Sale", "sale")      → true
    SameTag("sale", "sale ")     → false
    NormalizeKey("  Ada  ")      → "ada"
    HasIdPrefix("ORD-42", "ORD") → true
    JoinTags(["a", "", "b"])     → "a, b"

Every comparison you write must say WHICH comparison it means.

hint: string.Equals and StartsWith both take a StringComparison.
For a key you will store and look up later, invariant beats current
culture — the machine that writes it may not be the one that reads.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/05-strings-t.explanation:
Every string comparison in .NET picks one of two behaviours, and if
you do not choose, someone else's culture chooses for you.
ORDINAL compares the underlying UTF-16 code units: fast, exact, and
identical on every machine. CULTURE-AWARE comparison asks the
current locale how letters sort and fold, which is right for text a
human reads and wrong for anything a program keys on.
Tags, ids, file names, protocol tokens and dictionary keys are all
the second kind of string. Use StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase to
fold case without inviting the locale in — and remember the famous
counterexample: in Turkish, lowercasing 'I' does NOT give 'i', so
comparing a.ToLower() with b.ToLower() compares two different
strings on a Turkish machine and passes every test on yours.
NormalizeKey uses ToLowerInvariant for the same reason: the key you
write today may be read by a process in another locale tomorrow.
JoinTags shows the composition habit: filter, then join. string.Join
puts the separator BETWEEN items only, so filtering first is what
keeps ", " from appearing where a blank used to be.
Rule of thumb: reach for Ordinal / OrdinalIgnoreCase by default, and
only use culture comparison for sorting text you are about to show
to a person.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/06-pattern-m.instructions:
**Concepts:** switch expressions · property patterns · relational patterns  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

The shipping desk has rules, and rules are what switch expressions
are for. An Order (defined at the BOTTOM of this file) has a weight
in grams, a destination, and whether it is express.

    ShippingBand(0)       → "free"      (nothing to ship)
    ShippingBand(999)     → "small"     (1..999)
    ShippingBand(5000)    → "medium"    (1000..9999)
    ShippingBand(20000)   → "pallet"    (10000 and up)
    ShippingBand(-1)      → "invalid"

    Describe(new Order(500, "NL", false)) → "standard to NL"
    Describe(new Order(500, "NL", true))  → "express to NL"
    Describe(new Order(0, "NL", true))    → "nothing to ship"

Write both with switch expressions — no if/else chains. That is the
exercise: the shape, not the answer.

hint: relational patterns (less-than, greater-than) combine with
and / or / not. A property pattern looks like { Weight: 0 } or
{ IsExpress: true, Destination: var d }.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/06-pattern-m.explanation:
A switch expression is a chain of "shape produces value" arms tried
top to bottom, and the first match wins. That ordering is doing real
work: because the negative case is tested first, every later arm can
assume a non-negative number, and because "less than 1000" comes
before "less than 10000", no arm has to restate the lower bound. The
same rules written as ifs need a two-sided range in the middle, and
that is exactly where off-by-one bugs live.
Relational patterns and the combinators and / or / not let you say a
range once. The discard arm _ is "everything else"; without one the
compiler warns when your arms are not exhaustive, which is a feature
worth leaning on rather than silencing.
Describe uses PROPERTY patterns: { Weight: 0 } matches on a member
without a cast or a null check, and { IsExpress: true } reads as the
business rule it encodes. Ordering matters again — the empty order is
matched before the express/standard split, which is why an express
order of nothing still ships nothing.
Why prefer this to if/else: a switch expression is an EXPRESSION, so
every path must produce a value. You cannot forget to return and you
cannot fall out of the bottom with nothing assigned — two common
logic bugs, made unrepresentable.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/07-tuples-an.instructions:
**Concepts:** value tuples · named elements · deconstruction  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Sometimes a method has two answers and inventing a class for them is
ceremony. A value tuple with NAMED elements says it in one line:

    MinMax([3, 1, 4])       → (Min: 1, Max: 4)
    ParseLine("widget x3")  → (Name: "widget", Quantity: 3)
    Format(("widget", 3))   → "3 x widget"

MinMax on an empty sequence returns (0, 0) — there is no answer, and
throwing would make the caller's life harder than it needs to be.
ParseLine splits on the last " x"; a line with no quantity means 1.

hint: return (a, b) and the tuple builds itself. On the way back out
you can deconstruct: var (min, max) = MinMax(...).
csbootcamp/01-language-core/07-tuples-an.explanation:
A ValueTuple is a struct the compiler writes for you. Naming the
elements in the return type costs nothing at runtime — the names are
metadata — and it turns result.Item1 into result.Min, which is the
whole point. Nobody remembers what Item2 meant.
MinMax enumerates ONCE into a list before asking two questions. The
obvious version, numbers.Min() and numbers.Max(), walks the sequence
twice, and on an IEnumerable that is a database query, a file read,
or a generator, walking twice is a correctness bug rather than a
performance note.
ParseLine uses LastIndexOf so a name containing " x" survives, and
int.TryParse so a malformed quantity falls back rather than throws.
This is the parse-do-not-validate habit in miniature: turn a loose
string into a shaped value once, at the edge.
When does a tuple stop being right? When the pair escapes the method
that made it — a tuple in a public API, a field, or a dictionary
value is a record waiting to be born. Tuples are for local
plumbing; records are for things that have a name in the domain.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/08-out-and-r.instructions:
**Concepts:** out parameters · ref parameters · TryParse  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

.NET's answer to "this might not work and I do not want an
exception" is the Try pattern: return bool, hand the value back
through an out parameter, and set it to default on failure.

    TryParsePort("8080", out var p)  → true,  p = 8080
    TryParsePort("70000", out var p) → false, p = 0   (out of range)
    TryParsePort("abc", out var p)   → false, p = 0
    TryParsePort(null, out var p)    → false, p = 0

A valid port is 1 to 65535 inclusive. Then two more:

    Swap(ref a, ref b)               swaps the caller's variables
    CountAndSum([1,2,3], out count)  → 6, count = 3

hint: int.TryParse already does half of TryParsePort. An out
parameter MUST be assigned on every path before you return — the
compiler enforces it, including the failure path.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/08-out-and-r.explanation:
The three keywords answer three different questions.
OUT means "I will give this to you" — the caller need not initialise
it, and the method MUST assign it on every path. That last rule is
why the failure path here writes 0 rather than leaving the value
alone: a Try method that fails and leaves a stale number behind is
the source of a whole family of bugs, because callers read the value
after ignoring the bool.
REF means "we share this variable" — assignments inside are visible
outside, which is what makes Swap possible at all. Passing a class
by value already lets you mutate the OBJECT; ref is what lets you
replace the caller's variable itself.
IN (not used here) means "I promise not to change it" and passes a
large struct without copying.
Note the layering: TryParsePort delegates the hard part to
int.TryParse and adds one domain rule (the range). Validation that
wraps a parser, rather than re-implementing it, is how you keep
edge cases someone else already got right.
When NOT to use out: when there is no bool. CountAndSum works, but
returning (Sum, Count) as a named tuple reads better and composes;
out shines specifically in the Try pattern, where the bool is the
point and the value is the payload.
Discards keep the intent visible: `out _` says "there is a value and
I genuinely do not want it".

csbootcamp/01-language-core/09-boxing-an.instructions:
**Concepts:** boxing · object.Equals · type checks  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A settings bag stores whatever the config file had: object values
that might be an int, a string, a bool. Three helpers over that bag,
and every one of them meets boxing:

    AreEqual(1, 1)          → true    (two boxes, one value)
    AreEqual(1, 1L)         → false   (int and long are not the same)
    AreEqual("a", "a")      → true
    AreEqual(null, null)    → true
    SumInts([1, "x", 2])    → 3       (skip what is not an int)
    CountDistinct([1,1,"1",2]) → 3    ("1" is not 1)

All three must work without throwing on any input, including null.

hint: object.Equals(a, b) is the static one — it handles both nulls
and calls the right Equals underneath. A type test with a pattern
(`value is int n`) both checks and unboxes in one step.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/09-boxing-an.explanation:
Boxing is what happens when a value type is stored in a reference
slot: the runtime allocates an object on the heap and copies the
value into it. `object x = 1;` is a heap allocation, and every one
of those boxes is a separate object.
That is why `==` is the wrong operator here. On two `object`
variables, `==` is REFERENCE comparison — it asks "the same box?",
not "the same value?" — so two boxes each holding 1 compare unequal
and the bug only shows up once the values stop being cached or
interned. `object.Equals(a, b)` (the static two-argument form) is
null-safe on both sides and dispatches to the real Equals, which for
int compares numbers and for string compares characters.
int versus long is the second lesson: boxed values keep their exact
type, and Int32.Equals(Int64) is false. No numeric conversion
happens once a value is inside a box, which is exactly why config
bags that "worked in the test" break on a value that arrived as a
long from JSON.
`value is int n` is the modern unbox: it checks the type and gives
you the value in one step, with no cast that can throw and no
double type check. Prefer it to `if (v is int) { (int)v }`.
Distinct() uses EqualityComparer<object>.Default, which lands on the
same Equals — so 1 and "1" stay two values, and null counts once.
The performance note worth carrying: boxing allocates. A hot loop
over object is a garbage-collection problem, and it is why the BCL
has generic overloads everywhere. Reach for object only when the
type genuinely is not known until runtime.

csbootcamp/01-language-core/10-spans-wit.instructions:
**Concepts:** ReadOnlySpan<char> · slicing · parsing without Split  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A log parser runs over millions of lines, and every Split() and
Substring() it does allocates a new string that the collector then
has to clean up. A Span is a WINDOW onto memory you already have:
slicing it copies nothing.

    SumCsv("1,2,3")        → 6
    SumCsv("")             → 0
    TrimQuotes("\"hi\"")   → hi        (only if both quotes are there)
    IsPalindrome("racecar")→ true

Write all three against ReadOnlySpan<char>, using no Split, no
Substring, and no ToString except where a test needs one.

hint: a string converts to a ReadOnlySpan<char> implicitly.
span.IndexOf(',') finds the next separator, span[..i] is everything
before it, span[(i + 1)..] everything after. int.Parse accepts a
span directly.
csbootcamp/01-language-core/10-spans-wit.explanation:
A Span is a pointer and a length: it describes a region of memory
that belongs to somebody else. Slicing produces another pointer and
length, so `span[..i]` costs nothing while `text.Substring(0, i)`
copies characters into a fresh string. Over a million log lines
that difference is the whole garbage-collection bill.
SumCsv walks the line one separator at a time: find the comma, parse
the head, keep the tail, repeat, and parse whatever is left at the
end. int.Parse has span overloads precisely so this loop never has
to build a string. Trimming is a slice too.
TrimQuotes shows why "span in, span out" is the right signature: the
result is a WINDOW onto the caller's characters, not a copy, so
nothing is allocated until somebody actually needs a string (which
is what the tests do with ToString). Check both ends before
trimming, or an unmatched quote silently eats a real character.
IsPalindrome is the two-pointer walk with no reversal and no copy —
compare the ends, step inward, stop when they cross.
The rules that come with the power: a ref struct like Span cannot be
a field of a class, cannot be captured by a lambda, cannot be used
across an await, and must not outlive the memory it points at. If
you need any of those, you need a string or an array — and the
compiler will tell you so rather than letting you dangle.
